questions.question: Why does disaggregated prefill/decode improve efficiency compared to colocated serving?
options: Disaggregation allows each GPU to run at a higher clock speed
Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound; colocation wastes one resource on each GPU
Disaggregation allows the KV cache to be shared across all requests globally
It enables FP4 quantization on decode GPUs while prefill uses FP8
questions.explanation: Prefill (processing the input prompt) is compute-bound; decode (generating output tokens) is memory-bandwidth-bound. Running both on the same GPU means the GPU is simultaneously underutilizing compute (during decode) and underutilizing memory bandwidth (during prefill). Separate pools allow each to be optimized independently.

questions.question: What protocol does disaggregated serving use to transfer KV cache between prefill and decode pools?
options: gRPC over TCP
NIXL (RDMA/InfiniBand or TCP fallback)
NFS/POSIX file system
Redis pub/sub
questions.explanation: NIXL is the KV cache transfer protocol in disaggregated serving architectures. It uses RDMA/InfiniBand when available for maximum bandwidth, with TCP as a fallback. The choice of transport matters because KV cache can be gigabytes per request.

questions.question: NVIDIA Dynamo is described as sitting above vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM. What does its Planner Profiler and SLA Planner do?
options: They recompile model kernels at runtime to optimize for current hardware utilization
They measure workload characteristics and auto-configure prefill:decode ratios to meet SLOs
They profile memory usage across all engines and redistribute KV cache blocks
They route requests to the cheapest available provider in real time
questions.explanation: Dynamo's Planner Profiler measures the incoming workload (prompt lengths, request rates, output lengths) and feeds the SLA Planner, which automatically configures the ratio of prefill-to-decode GPU pool size to meet the target SLO.

questions.question: When does disaggregation NOT pay off?
options: When running on NVIDIA H100 hardware instead of GB200
For prompts under 512 tokens with short outputs — the KV transfer cost exceeds the gain
When the cluster has more than 16 GPUs
When using vLLM instead of SGLang as the serving engine
questions.explanation: Short prompts (< 512 tokens) with short outputs generate a small KV cache. The NIXL transfer overhead — even over InfiniBand — exceeds the compute savings from separating the pools. The transfer tax dominates the gain.

questions.question: How does llm-d differ from NVIDIA Dynamo in its operational model?
options: llm-d only supports vLLM while Dynamo supports all engines
llm-d is Kubernetes-native with prefill/decode/router as independent Services and per-role HPA; Dynamo is an orchestration layer above serving engines
llm-d is open-source while Dynamo is proprietary
llm-d handles model routing while Dynamo handles hardware provisioning
questions.explanation: llm-d (Red Hat + AWS) is Kubernetes-native: each of prefill, decode, and router runs as independent Kubernetes Services with separate HPAs using inference-specific signals (queue depth for prefill, KV utilization for decode). Dynamo is an orchestration layer that sits above existing serving engines.

questions.question: What are the reported annual savings when switching from colocated to disaggregated serving on a $2M inference spend?
options: $50-100K (5% savings)
$1.5M (75% savings)
questions.explanation: The lesson cites an internal rollup suggesting 30-40% savings on $2M-class inference spend when switching to disaggregated serving with Dynamo at constant SLA — approximately $600-800K per year. This is presented as an order-of-magnitude anchor, not a single published case study.
